chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Cecil Scott's Syncopaters: Frankie Newton, Don Frye and Savoy showmanship
summary: Horace met Dickie Wells in Cecil Scott's Springfield band, which battled his Collegians in Ohio; trumpeter Frankie Newton replaced Bill Coleman and the band later stood next to Chick Webb at the Savoy.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Great big guy. Well, he took Coleman Johnson's place when Cole went to Europe with this band. They had played the Savoy Ballroom, Frankie Newton would do his little arranging, and (inaudible) mentioned. He could play, man. And he was such a nice guy. And he's passed. Boy! But this is the band that I first met Dickie Wells in, the trombonist. And, of course, we used to play little battles of music, you know, and they were one of the greatest attractions in the state of Ohio, the buckeye state. They were well known. Sometimes I'd be fighting and playing a dance at the same town, and Cecil Scott and his Syncopaters were there. I didn't think we were going to have anybody, but it worked out pretty good, you know?

Well, we became friends, and, of course, Don Frye, the pianist in that band, and I are very good friends. Don could always play, and I liked Don's style -- swinging, you know? It seems like -- let's see -- did I miss anybody else in that band? No, I think that's about it. Well, they had a couple of other guys, but these are the guys that I knew. they had seven or eight pieces, but they kept busy, played all the time. Believe me, they went to New York, and they were

on the bandstand next to Chick Webb at the Savoy Ballroom. Of course, you can attribute that to Cecil Scott, which he stayed in New York (inaudible) for quite a few years. In fact, I think he died there.

But he was a showman. And He kept that group together. At the Savoy, (inaudible) Chick Webb would play with Ella (inaudible) and everything. Then Cecil Scott would direct the band and sell with that clarinet and that cape and hat (inaudible) and everything. He would play the baritone saxophone, and he would do what they a thing called those days, the slapstick, you know. (Sounds) (inaudible), you know. People would eat that up.
